Guided Inquiry

The setup

Two frictionless tracks start at the same height and end at the ground. The blue one is a gentle curve; the pink one is steeper with a dip. Both bodies have the same mass and are released from rest.

Beside the scene are three bars: KE, PE, and their Total. Watch the Total as you advance.

Predict — do they cross the finish at the same speed?

Same height dropped, but the pink track is longer and its shape is completely different. What will you see when both bodies reach the ground?

Watch the total

Press ▶ Play. As each body descends, its PE bar drains into the KE bar joule for joule. The Total bar does not move — not by a pixel. That is what conservation of energy looks like.

Notice too that both bodies reach the ground at 14.007 m/s, even though they do not arrive together. Time differs; final speed does not.

Change the height

Slide the release height. The Total bar jumps to mgh₀ — the new starting energy — and the finish speed follows v = √(2gh). Doubling h multiplies v by only √2 ≈ 1.41, not by 2.

Change the mass instead: the bars scale, but the finish speed is unchanged. Mass cancels in ½mv² = mgh.

The whole power of the energy method

Neither body's trajectory was solved. No forces resolved along the track, no time integration. Conservation of energy answered the question about the end state without ever describing the motion in between.

This is why the energy method solves problems the force method cannot: the answer at the bottom depends only on the height at the top.

01

At a glance

Two balls slide down frictionless tracks of different shape from the same release height, while three bars keep a running count of the energy. It shows when you can find a speed from energy alone, without working out forces or times.

What you'll learn

  • How a ball's kinetic and potential energy are related as it moves down a track.
  • How the speed at the finish depends on the release height h₀, the mass m and the shape of the track.
  • How to turn a height into a speed with one equation.
Two frictionless tracks of different shape, one release height, and three energy bars beside them.

What's on screen

  • Gentle track (blue): a smooth curve from the release line to the ground.
  • Steep + dip track (pink): a steeper curve that goes below the ground line before it reaches the finish.
  • Dashed lines: the release height h₀ (top) and the ground, y = 0 (bottom). Both tracks end at FINISH.
  • Energy bars (right): KE, PE and Total in joules. They follow the blue ball.
See itPress Play and watch both balls go down. Watch for: both balls starting from the dashed release line, and the KE and PE bars changing as the blue ball moves.

03

Energy changes form but the total stays fixed

Released from rest at height h₀, a ball starts with potential energy mgh₀ and no kinetic energy. Going down the track it trades one for the other:

½mv² + mgh = mgh₀
Kinetic energy + potential energy = the starting energy.

Here h is the ball's height above the ground line. The track is frictionless and pushes at right angles to the motion, so it does no work; only gravity does, and that is already counted in mgh. For m = 2 kg and h₀ = 10 m the Total is 2 × 9.81 × 10 = 196.2 J. At h = 5 m the ball holds 98.1 J of each kind.

See itPress Play and read the three bars as the blue ball goes down. Set Speed to 0.5× to follow it more easily. Watch for: the PE bar draining into the KE bar while the Total bar stays level at 196.2 J.
04

Speed depends only on the height dropped

Setting the kinetic energy equal to the potential energy given up, ½mv² = mg(h₀ − h), the mass cancels and

v = √(2g(h₀ − h))
The speed depends on the height dropped, h₀ − h.

Nothing in this equation refers to the length or the shape of the track, only to how far the ball is below its release height. At the finish h = 0, so

  • v = √(2gh₀) = √(2 × 9.81 × 10) = 14.007 m/s for the opening settings.
  • The At the finish panel shows this number for the current h₀, and a badge with it appears at FINISH on each track.
See itPress Play and wait until both balls have finished. Watch for: one badge at FINISH on each track, both reading v = 14.007 m/s.
05

The path changes the time, not the speed

Two tracks that drop the same height give the same speed at the finish, yet the balls need not arrive together: speed is fixed by height, but the time depends on how long the path is and how fast the ball is moving along it.

Both tracks drop the same h₀ to the ground line. The pink one goes below that line first and climbs back up to the finish.

The pink track is longer, and it dips about 1.6 m below the ground line at the opening settings. There the drop is h₀ + 1.6 m, so the pink ball briefly reaches about 15.1 m/s. It slows again as it climbs, and is back to 14.007 m/s at the finish. At 10 m the two balls arrive a fraction of a second apart.

See itPress Play and follow the pink ball through its dip. Watch for: the pink ball dropping below the ground line and the two balls reaching FINISH at slightly different moments, with the same speed on both badges.
06

Speed grows as the square root of the height

Because v = √(2gh₀), the speed grows more slowly than the height.

h₀final speed vTotal energy mgh₀ (m = 2 kg)
5 m9.905 m/s98.1 J
10 m14.007 m/s196.2 J
20 m19.809 m/s392.4 J

Doubling h₀ doubles the energy but multiplies the speed by only √2 ≈ 1.41. To double the speed you need four times the height.

See itSet h₀ to 20 m and press Play. Watch for: the Total bar reaching 392.4 J, and both finish badges reading v = 19.809 m/s.
07

Mass sets the energy but cancels from the speed

The mass appears on both sides of ½mv² = mgh, so it cancels from the speed. It still sets how much energy there is to exchange.

mTotal energy mgh₀ (h₀ = 10 m)final speed v
0.5 kg49.1 J14.007 m/s
2 kg196.2 J14.007 m/s
5 kg490.5 J14.007 m/s

A heavier ball is pulled harder by gravity, but it also has more inertia to move, and the two effects cancel exactly. The bars grow in proportion to m while the speed stays put.

See itSet the mass to 5 kg and press Play. Watch for: the Total bar growing to 490.5 J while both finish badges still read v = 14.007 m/s.
08

Where it matters

  • Roller coasters. With friction and air drag ignored, a car's speed at any point depends on how far that point lies below the highest point it has reached. That is why each hill after the first lift is lower.
  • Pendulums. The bob's speed at the lowest point is √(2gh), with h the height it was released above that point.
  • Where it stops working. Friction and drag turn mechanical energy into heat, so the energy equation needs an extra term for the work they do. A ball that rolls instead of sliding also stores energy in its spin: a solid ball rolling down a height h reaches √(10gh/7), about 0.85 of the sliding speed.
  • What it cannot give. Energy gives the speed at a point, but not the time taken or the force from the track. Those need Newton's laws.
09

Summary

In one line. On a frictionless track a ball trades height for speed, and an energy equation turns that trade into numbers.

Key points

  • ½mv² + mgh = mgh₀: the Total stays at its starting value.
  • The speed at any point is √(2g × height dropped), whatever the path.
  • Mass cancels from the speed; doubling h₀ multiplies it by √2.

Common mix-ups

  • "A longer or steeper path must change the final speed." Only the height dropped matters. The path changes the time.
  • "A heavier ball finishes faster." Its energy is larger, but the mass cancels from ½mv² = mgh.
  • "Twice the height gives twice the speed." It gives √2 times the speed, because v goes as √h₀.

Things to try on your own

  • Set h₀ so that the finish speed is close to 10 m/s, then check it with h₀ = v²/(2g).
  • Compare the Total at 0.5 kg and at 5 kg, and divide one by the other.
  • Watch the pink ball in its dip and compare its speed there with the 14.007 m/s on the badge.
